name: FARO
description: Faro is an iconic 19th-century banking game immortalized in American frontier lore as the favorite of gamblers like Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday. Known colloquially as 'Bucking the Tiger' (from the tiger illustrations on dealing boxes), it is a game of pure chance where players wager on which card ranks will be drawn from a specially-designed dealing box. Unlike poker, Faro was prized for its transparency and relatively low house edge, allowing players to track all remaining cards using a public tool called a 'Case Keeper'.

content.text: Faro is an iconic 19th-century banking game immortalized in American frontier lore as the favorite of gamblers like Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday. Known colloquially as 'Bucking the Tiger' (from the tiger illustrations on dealing boxes), it is a game of pure chance where players wager on which card ranks will be drawn from a specially-designed dealing box. Unlike poker, Faro was prized for its transparency and relatively low house edge, allowing players to track all remaining cards using a public tool called a 'Case Keeper'.

Faro descended from the French game Pharaon (1688), which itself derived from the Italian game Bassetta introduced to Paris in the early 17th century. Introduced to the USA via New Orleans, it spread rapidly across the frontier during the 19th century.
Any number of players can bet against a single Banker. Traditionally 1-10 players.
Standard 52-card deck. Card ranks: Ace (low) through King (high).

1. **Dealing Box**: Special box with a slot to expose card faces while preventing double-dealing. 2. **Layout**: Pasteboard or cloth with 13 card ranks (Ace through King) where players place bets. 3. **Case Keeper**: An abacus-like device with beads to track which cards have been drawn from the deck. 4. **Coppers**: Hexagonal tokens placed on bets to indicate 'losing' prediction.
Dealer (the Banker) shuffles the deck and places it in the dealing box. The first card exposed (the 'Soda') is a dead card and is removed from play. Betting then begins.

items.text: Stuss (Jewish Faro): Simplified version without a dealing box; cards drawn from hand. House advantage dramatically increases: on splits, House takes ALL bets (not just half). Popular in Jewish communities.
Pharaon (Original French): Earlier version with more complex betting rules. Players could make larger bets and more exotic wagers.
Blind Faro: Played without a Case Keeper; players rely on memory alone to track remaining cards. Dramatically increases House advantage.
Calling the Turn: Specialty bet available when 3 cards remain. Player predicts exact order of final three cards. Pays 4:1 (sometimes 3:1).
